questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has a 1 day history of lower abdominal pain, worse on the right, with anorexia and loose stools. Her pregnancy test is negative. With her right hip and knee flexed, internal rotation of the hip causes pain deep in her right lower abdomen. Her temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely position of her inflamed appendix?
questions.e: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign: a pelvic appendix irritates obturator internus. Pelvic appendicitis can also cause diarrhoea.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely position of her inflamed appendix? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Internal rotation of the **flexed** hip = **obturator sign**, which means the appendix lies against obturator internus in the **pelvis**.

elim: Gives typical RIF tenderness; the hip sign points elsewhere.
Not linked to a positive obturator sign.
Gives a positive psoas sign (pain on hip hyperextension) and flank pain.
Gives right upper quadrant pain.

steps.x: **B. Pelvic.** Obturator sign = pelvic appendix; psoas sign = retrocaecal appendix.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a 2 day history of right-sided abdominal pain and anorexia. His temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. The surgical registrar lies him on his left side and extends his right hip backwards; this reproduces his pain. Urinalysis is normal.
questions.q: Which sign has been elicited?
questions.e: Pain on hyperextension of the right hip stretches psoas, which lies against a retrocaecal appendix: the psoas sign.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which sign has been elicited? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Hip hyperextension** stretches **psoas**. An inflamed retrocaecal appendix lies on it.

elim: Periumbilical bruising in haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
Pain on inspiration with RUQ palpation in cholecystitis.
Pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip.
RIF pain on palpating the left iliac fossa.

steps.x: **D. Psoas sign.** Hip hyperextension pain = psoas sign = retrocaecal appendix.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 24 hour history of abdominal pain that started around her umbilicus and is now in the right iliac fossa. She has no appetite and vomited once. Her last period was 2 weeks ago and her urine beta-hCG is negative. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She is tender with guarding in the right iliac fossa.

visual.title: Where the pain moved
visual.caption: Central pain that has settled in the right iliac fossa.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Central pain migrating to the RIF with anorexia, vomiting, low-grade fever and RIF guarding is acute appendicitis; the negative beta-hCG excludes an ectopic pregnancy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: started around her umbilicus and is now in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: **Migratory pain** central to RIF + **anorexia** + fever. The pregnancy test has done its job.

elim: Excluded by the negative beta-hCG.
Sudden severe unilateral pain, not central pain that migrates.
Bilateral lower pain, discharge and cervical excitation.
Sudden pain mid-cycle without anorexia or migration.

steps.x: **A. Acute appendicitis.** Migratory pain + anorexia + negative hCG in a young woman = appendicitis.

questions.stem: A 10 year old boy has an 18 hour history of abdominal pain and two episodes of vomiting. He winces when his mother drives over a speed bump. His temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 120 bpm. He is tender with guarding at a point one third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. Urine dipstick is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Localised guarding at McBurney's point with fever, vomiting and pain on movement is acute appendicitis; a normal urine dip makes UTI unlikely.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: winces when his mother drives over a speed bump
one third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine
steps.x: Pain on jolting = **peritonism**. Guarding at **McBurney's point**. Urine is clear.

elim: Diarrhoea predominant, with diffuse mild tenderness and no guarding.
Usually under 2 years old, with redcurrant jelly stools.
Follows a viral illness, with high fever and less localised tenderness.
The urine dipstick is normal.

steps.x: **A. Acute appendicitis.** Fever + McBurney's point guarding + normal urine = appendicitis.

questions.stem: A 14 year old girl had 2 days of right iliac fossa pain that suddenly eased, followed by 3 days of feeling unwell. She now has a swinging fever up to 39.2°C, rigors and tenderness in the right iliac fossa. The rest of the abdomen is soft. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm. Ultrasound shows a 4 cm fluid collection beside the caecum.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pain that eases suddenly suggests perforation; a swinging fever with a localised RIF collection means the infection has been walled off as an appendicular abscess.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: The rest of the abdomen is soft
steps.x: Sudden easing = **perforation**. **Swinging fever** + collection + soft abdomen elsewhere = the pus has been **walled off**.

elim: A chronic course with diarrhoea and weight loss.
No collection, and no swinging fever with rigors.
Sudden severe pain; no fluid collection with swinging fever.
Sudden epigastric pain with generalised peritonitis.

steps.x: **A. Appendicular abscess.** Swinging fever after a perforated appendix = appendicular abscess.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has a 1 day history of central abdominal pain that moved to the right iliac fossa this morning. He has vomited twice and has no appetite. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. The examining doctor presses deeply in the right iliac fossa and then releases suddenly.

visual.title: Site of tenderness
visual.caption: Localised tenderness in the right iliac fossa.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
o: Rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa
questions.e: Once the parietal peritoneum over McBurney's point is inflamed, sudden release of pressure causes sharp pain: rebound tenderness, a sign of localised peritonitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: moved to the right iliac fossa
steps.x: The pain has localised, so the **parietal peritoneum** is inflamed. Sudden release jolts it.

elim: Periumbilical bruising, seen in haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
Flank bruising in retroperitoneal haemorrhage.
RUQ sign of cholecystitis.
A sign of ascites.

steps.x: **D. Rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa.** Localised RIF peritonism in appendicitis gives rebound tenderness.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has right iliac fossa pain for 20 hours with anorexia. His temperature is 37.7°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. Urinalysis is normal. The doctor wants to know which feature of the history best suggests the peritoneum is inflamed.
questions.q: Which feature of the history most supports localised peritonitis?
o: Pain worse on moving and coughing
questions.e: Inflamed parietal peritoneum hurts when it is moved, so patients with appendicitis lie still and pain is worse on moving or coughing.

steps.x: This asks for a feature that supports a mechanism (peritoneal irritation), not for the diagnosis.

clues: right iliac fossa pain for 20 hours
steps.x: Peritonitis = pain on **any movement** of the peritoneum: walking, coughing, bumps in the road. Colic makes people writhe.

elim: Typical of ureteric or biliary colic, not peritonitis.
Typical of pancreatitis or pericarditis.
Suggests pancreatitis or a leaking aneurysm.
Typical of a duodenal ulcer.

steps.x: **E. Pain worse on moving and coughing.** Pain worse on moving or coughing = peritoneal irritation (appendicitis).

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has a 1 day history of migratory right iliac fossa pain, fever and anorexia. CT abdomen and pelvis shows a dilated, thick-walled appendix with surrounding fat stranding and a small, round, calcified opacity at the base of the appendix lumen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his appendicitis?
questions.e: Appendicitis is caused by luminal obstruction, most commonly a faecolith, which can appear as a calcified appendicolith on CT. Lymphoid hyperplasia is more common in children.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his appendicitis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **calcified** plug in the lumen of an adult appendix = **faecolith**.

elim: A rare cause of obstruction; would appear as a soft tissue mass.
A rare cause; not seen as a calcified opacity.
Rare; the round calcified opacity is typical of a faecolith.
The usual cause in children, often after a viral illness; not calcified.

steps.x: **C. Faecolith.** Adults: faecolith; children: lymphoid hyperplasia.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a 2 day history of abdominal pain, now in the right lower abdomen, with anorexia, nausea and three loose stools. He has never had bowel problems. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. He has right iliac fossa tenderness and guarding.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Anorexia, nausea, mild diarrhoea, fever, RIF guarding and raised inflammatory markers fit acute appendicitis. Diarrhoea does not exclude it.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Localised **RIF guarding**, fever, **anorexia** and raised **WCC/CRP**. Diarrhoea is a recognised feature of appendicitis.

elim: No history of chronic diarrhoea, weight loss or prior bowel problems.
Usually left iliac fossa pain in older patients.
Diarrhoea is mild; localised guarding with fever points to appendicitis.
Loin-to-groin colic and haematuria; no guarding or raised CRP.

steps.x: **A. Acute appendicitis.** Do not let diarrhoea talk you out of appendicitis when there is RIF guarding.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman with suspected appendicitis is examined by a medical student. Her pain started centrally 18 hours ago and is now sharp and well localised. The registrar asks the student where on the abdomen the tenderness should be maximal.

visual.title: Right iliac fossa
visual.caption: McBurney's point sits in the right iliac fossa.

questions.q: Where is McBurney's point most likely to be?
o: Below the right costal margin in the midclavicular line
One third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus
questions.e: McBurney's point lies one third of the way along a line from the right ASIS to the umbilicus, over the base of the appendix, where the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.

steps.x: An anatomy question: where is the classic point of tenderness?
Sharp, localised pain = **parietal peritoneum** over the appendix base, which is at **McBurney's point**.

elim: This is where Murphy's sign is tested (gallbladder).
Palpated in Rovsing's sign, but the tenderness is felt on the right.
Tender in pyelonephritis.
Tender in cystitis or a pelvic process.

steps.x: **C. One third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.** McBurney's point: one third from the right ASIS to the umbilicus.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy has had abdominal pain for 5 days. His parents thought it was a stomach bug. He now has a swinging fever up to 38.9°C and a tender, firm, fixed mass in the right iliac fossa. His pulse rate is 124 bpm. His white cell count is 18.4 × 10⁹/L and CRP 190 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A late presentation with a palpable RIF mass and swinging fever is an appendix mass; ultrasound confirms it and looks for an abscess.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: mass in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Late presentation (**5 days**), **palpable RIF mass**, **swinging fever**: appendicitis that has been walled off.

elim: Usually under 2 years, with colicky pain and redcurrant jelly stool; not a swinging fever.
Possible but rare; a late-presenting appendicitis is far more likely.
No palpable mass or swinging fever.
A painless flank mass in a well child.

steps.x: **A. Appendix mass.** Late appendicitis + palpable RIF mass + swinging fever = appendix mass.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl has had abdominal pain for 3 days that began around her umbilicus. Today she is lethargic and will not move. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 152 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg and capillary refill 4 seconds. Her whole abdomen is rigid and tender with absent bowel sounds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Untreated appendicitis progresses to necrosis and perforation; generalised rigidity with sepsis means perforated appendicitis needing resuscitation and urgent surgery. Young children perforate more often.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Days of untreated pain, now a **rigid abdomen** and **septic shock**. Children perforate early.

elim: Can cause abdominal pain, but not a rigid abdomen with absent bowel sounds.
Does not cause a rigid abdomen.
Usually under 2 years old, with redcurrant jelly stool.
Never causes generalised peritonitis.

steps.x: **E. Perforated appendicitis.** Generalised peritonitis + sepsis after RIF/central pain = perforated appendicitis: urgent surgery.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man with migratory right iliac fossa pain, anorexia and raised inflammatory markers undergoes laparoscopic appendicectomy. At operation the appendix looks inflamed. The team want to confirm the diagnosis and exclude an unexpected tumour.
questions.q: Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
questions.e: Appendicitis is a clinical diagnosis supported by blood tests and imaging, but it is confirmed by histology of the appendix, which also picks up incidental tumours such as carcinoid.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which investigation confirms the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Clinical and imaging findings **support**; **histology confirms**.

elim: Supports the diagnosis before surgery but does not confirm it.
Supports inflammation; not specific.
Supports the diagnosis; operator dependent.
Supports inflammation; not specific.

steps.x: **B. Histology of the resected appendix.** Gold standard for appendicitis = histology after appendicectomy.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has a 1 day history of right lower abdominal pain and anorexia. He has had no dysuria. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. He has tenderness in the right iliac fossa. Bloods have been sent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial bedside investigation?
questions.e: A urine dip is the first bedside test in RIF pain to look for a UTI or haematuria from a stone. In women a pregnancy test is also essential.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial bedside investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
First-line bedside tests in RIF pain: **urine dip** (all) and **beta-hCG** (women). He is a man.

elim: Not a bedside test and rarely helpful in appendicitis.
Not needed in a stable patient.
Imaging, not a bedside test.
For inflammatory bowel disease, not acute RIF pain.

steps.x: **E. Urine dipstick.** RIF pain: urine dip for everyone, beta-hCG for every woman of childbearing age.

questions.stem: A 7 year old girl has a 1 day history of central abdominal pain moving to the right iliac fossa, with vomiting. Her temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 118 bpm. She is tender in the right iliac fossa but the senior doctor is unsure of the diagnosis. Urine dipstick is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
questions.e: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging in children, pregnancy and young women with mild disease because it involves no radiation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **child** with an uncertain diagnosis: image without radiation.

elim: Rarely helpful in appendicitis.
Avoided first in children because of the radiation dose.
Invasive; imaging comes first when the diagnosis is uncertain.
Used in pregnancy if ultrasound is inconclusive; not first line in children.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound abdomen.** Children, pregnancy and young women: ultrasound first; adults: CT.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 2 day history of right iliac fossa pain, anorexia and fever. Her beta-hCG is negative and urine dip is normal. An ultrasound could not see the appendix. Twelve hours later her pain is worse and she has guarding. Her temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 112 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
questions.e: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast is used in adults when ultrasound is equivocal, the diagnosis is unclear or the patient deteriorates.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Adult, **equivocal ultrasound** and **deteriorating**: the next test is the more definitive one.

elim: Will not show the appendix.
Contraindicated in suspected acute appendicitis.
She is deteriorating; waiting is unsafe.
Looks at the ovaries, but she needs the appendix assessed.

steps.x: **C. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.** Equivocal USS or deteriorating adult = CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.

questions.stem: An 18 year old woman has a 12 hour history of mild right iliac fossa pain with nausea. Her temperature is 37.4°C and pulse rate 88 bpm. Her urine beta-hCG is negative. She has mild right iliac fossa tenderness without guarding. Her white cell count is 11.8 × 10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
questions.e: In a young woman with mild disease, ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis assesses the appendix and the ovaries without radiation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Young woman**, **mild** disease: ultrasound can see the appendix and the ovaries, with no radiation.

elim: Not useful for appendicitis.
Radiation; reserved for adults with an unclear picture after ultrasound.
For suspected stones.
Not first line.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound abdomen and pelvis.** Young woman with mild RIF pain = ultrasound abdomen and pelvis first.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has a 1 day history of migratory right iliac fossa pain, anorexia and a temperature of 37.9°C. His pulse rate is 100 bpm. He has guarding at McBurney's point. Blood tests are sent to support the clinical diagnosis.
questions.q: Which blood result is most likely?
o: Normal full blood count with a raised amylase
questions.e: Appendicitis is a bacterial inflammation, so the white cell count (neutrophils) and CRP usually rise. They support, not confirm, the diagnosis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which blood result is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Bacterial inflammation = **neutrophilia** and raised **CRP**.

elim: Suggests a viral illness.
Points to pancreatitis.
A cholestatic picture: biliary disease.
Suggests parasites or allergy.

steps.x: **B. Neutrophilia with a raised CRP.** Appendicitis bloods: raised WCC (neutrophils) and CRP.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has acute appendicitis diagnosed clinically and is listed for theatre in 4 hours. He is in severe pain and has vomited three times. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management while he waits for theatre?
o: Encourage oral fluids and a light meal
Nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia and an anti-emetic
Withhold analgesia until the consultant examines him
questions.e: Before appendicectomy: nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, anti-emetics if needed and prophylactic IV antibiotics.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management while he waits for theatre? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Going to theatre, **in pain**, **vomiting** and tachycardic: supportive care.

elim: He must be nil by mouth before a general anaesthetic.
Can worsen pain and risk perforation.
Contraindicated and irrelevant.
Analgesia does not mask the diagnosis and should never be withheld.

steps.x: **C. Nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia and an anti-emetic.** Pre-op appendicitis: NBM, IV fluids, analgesia, anti-emetic, IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a laparoscopic appendicectomy for uncomplicated acute appendicitis. She received one dose of IV amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole before surgery. At operation the appendix is inflamed but not perforated and there is no pus.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic plan after surgery?
o: Stop antibiotics and give no further doses
Two further IV doses 8 hours apart, completing 24 hours
questions.e: Uncomplicated appendicitis: IV antibiotics for 24 hours, one prophylactic dose before surgery and two doses 8 hourly after. Longer courses are for perforation or abscess.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic plan after surgery? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Uncomplicated** and **not perforated**: the short 24 hour course.

elim: Excessive for uncomplicated disease.
Far too long.
Not indicated.
The local regimen continues for 24 hours.

steps.x: **E. Two further IV doses 8 hours apart, completing 24 hours.** Uncomplicated appendicectomy: one dose pre-op, two 8-hourly post-op (24 hours).

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has an emergency laparoscopic appendicectomy. At operation the appendix is gangrenous and perforated, with pus in the pelvis, which is washed out. He received one dose of IV amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole at induction.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic plan after surgery?
o: Continue IV antibiotics for a longer treatment course
Give two more doses then stop at 24 hours
No further antibiotics because the source is removed
questions.e: Antibiotics are extended beyond 24 hours when the appendix has perforated or there is an abscess, because the peritoneum is contaminated.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic plan after surgery? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Perforated** with **pus**: this is no longer prophylaxis but treatment.

elim: Enough for uncomplicated disease, not for perforation with pus.
Contamination with pus needs a treatment course.
Lacks gram-negative and anaerobic cover.
Do not treat intra-abdominal infection.

steps.x: **A. Continue IV antibiotics for a longer treatment course.** Perforation or abscess = extend the antibiotic course.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has CT-confirmed uncomplicated acute appendicitis with no faecolith, abscess or perforation. She is stable with a temperature of 37.6°C and pulse rate 90 bpm. After discussing the risks of recurrence, she strongly prefers to avoid surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Antibiotics alone, with surgery if she does not improve
questions.e: In selected uncomplicated cases (no faecolith, abscess or perforation) antibiotics alone can be tried first-line, accepting a risk of recurrence; appendicectomy if it fails.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Uncomplicated**, no faecolith, patient **declines surgery**: the conservative option exists.

elim: Not indicated in acute appendicitis.
Appendicitis needs antibiotics or surgery.
Not needed and she declines surgery.
There is no collection to drain.

steps.x: **A. Antibiotics alone, with surgery if she does not improve.** Selected uncomplicated appendicitis: antibiotics alone is an option.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has had 3 days of right iliac fossa pain. Today it spread across his whole abdomen. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. His abdomen is rigid. He has received IV fluids and IV antibiotics. CT shows a perforated appendix with free fluid and free gas, and no discrete collection.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Antibiotics alone and review in 48 hours
questions.e: Generalised peritonitis or sepsis from a perforated appendix needs resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent surgery for source control.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Generalised peritonitis** and **sepsis** with no collection to drain: source control in theatre.

elim: Not safe with generalised peritonitis and sepsis.
There is no discrete collection to drain.
For a settled appendix mass, not acute peritonitis.
Supportive only; he needs source control.

steps.x: **E. Urgent appendicectomy and peritoneal washout.** Perforated appendicitis with peritonitis or sepsis = urgent surgery.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man presented with a 7 day history of right iliac fossa pain and a tender mass. Ultrasound showed an abscess, which was drained, and he was given IV antibiotics. Six weeks later he still has intermittent right iliac fossa pain and a small tender mass.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: An appendix mass or abscess is treated with IV antibiotics and drainage, then interval (delayed) appendicectomy if not improved after about 6 weeks.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: still has intermittent right iliac fossa pain
steps.x: Mass treated conservatively, **not improved at 6 weeks**: planned surgery.

elim: He still has symptoms and a mass.
Prolonged antibiotics do not treat the underlying appendix.
Not an emergency; a planned operation is safer.
No new collection is described.

steps.x: **D. Interval appendicectomy.** Appendix mass: IV antibiotics and drainage, then interval appendicectomy if not better at 6 weeks.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant has a 1 day history of migratory right-sided abdominal pain, anorexia and fever. Her temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 106 bpm. Ultrasound shows a non-compressible, thick-walled appendix. The fetal heart is heard.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Early laparoscopic appendicectomy is the definitive treatment, including in pregnancy, because perforation is far more dangerous to mother and fetus than surgery.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate definitive management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Confirmed appendicitis: the definitive treatment does not change in **pregnancy**.

elim: No obstetric indication for delivery at 16 weeks.
Delays definitive treatment; perforation in pregnancy risks fetal loss.
The diagnosis is confirmed; waiting risks perforation.
There is no collection.

steps.x: **C. Laparoscopic appendicectomy.** Definitive treatment of appendicitis = early laparoscopic appendicectomy, even in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man ignored right iliac fossa pain for 3 days. At operation the appendix has a black, gangrenous tip with a small hole leaking pus. Histology shows transmural necrosis behind an obstructing faecolith.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the perforation?
o: Acid-peptic ulceration of the appendix wall
Direct mechanical erosion by the faecolith
Ischaemic necrosis from rising intraluminal pressure
questions.e: Obstruction raises intraluminal pressure, which first impairs venous drainage and then arterial supply; bacterial overgrowth and ischaemia lead to necrosis and perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of the perforation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: transmural necrosis behind an obstructing faecolith
steps.x: Obstruction → **pressure** rises → venous then **arterial** compromise → **ischaemia** → necrosis → perforation.

elim: That is the mechanism of peptic ulcer perforation.
The faecolith obstructs; the wall dies from ischaemia.
Diverticular perforation happens in the colon.
No trauma was described.

steps.x: **C. Ischaemic necrosis from rising intraluminal pressure.** Appendix perforation = ischaemic necrosis from rising intraluminal pressure.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy has acute appendicitis. When the doctor presses deeply in his left iliac fossa, he feels pain in his right iliac fossa. He has guarding over McBurney's point. His temperature is 37.9°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for this sign?
o: Irritation of the inflamed peritoneum next to the appendix
Referred visceral pain via midgut afferents
questions.e: Rovsing's sign: pressing the LIF shifts bowel contents and gas towards the right, moving the inflamed parietal peritoneum next to the appendix. These signs all reflect localised peritoneal irritation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation for this sign? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: presses deeply in his left iliac fossa
pain in his right iliac fossa
steps.x: Pain is felt where the **inflamed peritoneum** is, not where the hand is.

elim: His left colon is not inflamed; the pain is felt on the right.
That explains the early central pain, not this sign.
That is the psoas sign on hip extension.
No urinary tract involvement.

steps.x: **B. Irritation of the inflamed peritoneum next to the appendix.** Rovsing's, psoas and obturator signs = localised peritoneal irritation by the appendix.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has a 6 day history of right iliac fossa pain. Her temperature swings to 38.8°C. Her abdomen is soft except for a tender mass in the right iliac fossa. CT shows a perforated appendix with a contained collection, wrapped in greater omentum, and no free fluid elsewhere.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason she has a localised collection rather than generalised peritonitis?
o: The infection was walled off by the omentum
The perforation sealed by itself immediately
questions.e: Whether perforation causes an abscess or generalised peritonitis depends on whether the body can wall off the infection, for example with the greater omentum.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man says his pain began 24 hours ago as a dull, vague ache around his navel that he could not point to. Overnight it became sharp and he can now point with one finger to the right iliac fossa.

questions.e: Early pain is visceral (distension, referred via midgut autonomic afferents to the umbilicus). Once the parietal peritoneum over McBurney's point is inflamed, somatic nerves give sharp, localised pain.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man is given IV amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole before appendicectomy. A pharmacy student asks why three drugs are used. The appendix contains a mixture of bowel bacteria that overgrow behind the obstruction.
questions.q: Which organisms is metronidazole mainly included to cover?

questions.e: Bowel flora overgrowing in the obstructed appendix include anaerobes (Bacteroides), gram-negatives (E. coli) and enterococci. Metronidazole covers the anaerobes, gentamicin the gram-negatives, amoxicillin the enterococci.
